title: What hisbonenus is: iyun, the depth of the concept, and daas
overview:
The book opens by asking what *hisbonenus* is. It is *iyun*, the inner side of *bina*: staying on a concept, cutting it into all its parts, until one reaches its depth, as against *girsa*, a passing glance. What the world calls concentration is only a *kli*. It gives no content, and taking it for the thing itself is "the whole mistake of idol worship". The depth of a concept in *bina* is only its *tamtzis*, like instant coffee, yet it is the fiftieth gate. Delving into it reaches the hidden *chachma*, the aquifer under every spring, and brings new light into the same book.

Innovation comes only within a field, from the people who know every part of the motor, never from going for *chiddushim*. The *navon*, like the Wright brothers with their bicycle chain, carries an idea from one field to another. The text runs from depth to length; the student goes the other way, one length at a time. *Daas* is the dive, not the floor of the ocean: it squeezes the whole mind onto one point, and *daas* and *bina* depend on each other.

sections.title: Hisbonenus is iyun, a long look, and not girsa, a passing glance
sections.summary: The chapter sets out to say what *hisbonenus* (contemplation) is in itself: a strong gaze into the depth of a matter, staying with it until it is understood in every detail. This is the inner side of *bina*, the *iyun* of the Talmud, as against *girsa*, which takes a thing in at first glance and soon forgets it.

sections.title: Width, length and depth: a concept is like a river, and iyun goes to its depth
sections.summary: Every concept has width (its explanation to every side), length (its descent into *meshalim*, down to a child) and depth (its essential point, like the current of a river, from which all the rest spreads). *Iyun* stays on a concept, slowly, to reach that depth; that is *hisbonenus*, with the doubled *nun*.

sections.title: Concentration is only a vessel; delving reaches the aquifer of chachma
sections.summary: What the world calls concentration, *ha'amakas hadaas*, is only a *kli*: it supplies no content, and taking it for the thing itself is the mistake of idol worship. Delving, *ma'amik*, goes past the explanation to the root of a concept, *taalumos chachma*, the one aquifer that every spring of wisdom comes from.

phrases.he: ונמצא בחינת העיון הזה הוא רק בחינת כלי לבחינת ההעמקה דבינה עצמה,
כי לכאורה בחינת העיון הזה נקרא העמקת הדעת בלשון בעולם,
phrases.en: This *iyun* is called by everybody contemplation or meditation.

phrases.he: ואינו כן,
phrases.en: It's not like that at all.

phrases.he: דהעמקת הדעת היינו בחינת כלי לבד לבוא לעומק של הענין ממש
phrases.en: So the *daas* is a *kli* to go deeper and deeper into it, but it's not the actual *omek*.

blocks.text:
This *iyun* is only a *kli* (vessel) for the depth of *bina* itself. The *iyun*, *bina sheb'bina*, is a *kli* for the *hasaga* (comprehension), the *omek hamusag*, *Keser* of *bina*: the learning is the *kli* for understanding the explanation.

The text doesn't say it here, but the chain goes on. *Hasaga* is understanding the explanation; it is the *kli* for *havana*, the outer *chachma*, seeing the thing itself. *Havana* is the *kli* for *taalumos chachma* (the hidden parts of *chachma*), seeing its inner essence, already a knowing, the *daas elyon* (higher knowledge) of *Keser*. That is the *kli* for *Radla*: experiencing the thing itself with no self-concept in it at all. Each lower level is a *kli* for a higher one. Now he goes down instead of up.

Now the text goes down. At first glance this *iyun* is what the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas* (concentration): contemplation or meditation, as when *Kuntres HaHisbonenus* is called the tract of meditation. But it is not so. Concentration is only a *kli*, to hold all these other things.

At each level *daas* is the outer *kli*. Without concentration *bina sheb'bina* won't work; going up from the *omek hamusag* to the *haskala* of the thing, or from the *havana* of *chachma* to the inner *chachma*, you also need *daas*. Once you know the explanation, you concentrate on it to go to the next, deeper level. So *daas* is a *kli* to go deeper, not the depth itself.

*Bina sheb'bina* is also an instrument, not the thing itself, but it works on the explanation and will actually get you there. *Daas* is not even that kind of instrument: "The *daas* is an instrument for an instrument."

This is the whole mistake of idol worship; that is what idol worship is. They see *daas* as the primary instrument. They may grant that concentration is not the thing itself, "the G-d realization or whatever they want to call it", but they go for it directly through *daas*: you think "G-d, G-d, G-d", and the concentration will get you there.

sensitivity.reason: Calls practices that seek G-d through concentration alone idol worship.

blocks.text: *Daas* is a *kli* not to reach the matter, only to go deeper into a matter you already have. *Daas* has to have content, and by itself it does not supply the content. The *bina sheb'bina* supplies it.

phrases.he: ולמעלה מזה הוא נקרא מעמיק,
שמגיע למעלה גם מן החכמה עצמה,

blocks.text:
Above this is *ma'amik* (delving), which is also concentration. On the *bina sheb'bina* it is the lower *ha'amakas hadaas*; *ma'amik* is concentrating on the *omek hamusag*, even held through a *mashal*, thinking it over and over, and this reaches higher even than *chachma* itself.

The outer *chachma* sees the explanation: not just the explanation, but what it is about, and still not *mamash* the actual thing. That is *taalumos chachma*. Once you are there you can even see what other things are about, because it gets to the root: "not just the thing, but the actual root of the thing."

blocks.title: The physicist and the root of physics
blocks.text: Take physics. There is the explanation. A real physicist understands more than the explanation. That doesn't mean he has the root of physics, something like metaphysics, the root that "will answer questions in other fields, also". That is *taalumos chachma*.

phrases.en: Even though the *chachma* is in a way of an *ayin* compared to the *omek nekudas hamusag sheb'bina*,

phrases.en: The hidden parts of the *chachma*.

blocks.text: Although *chachma* is the very *ayin* (nothing) of the concept, not yet in any particular explanation, while the *omek hamusag* is the depth *davka* of this particular explanation, "like a spring compared to a river", delving into the root of the concept reaches the root that draws forth the spring of *chachma*.

A scientist can look deeply into physics and get all kinds of insights, but he won't look deeper: how did the whole thing come into existence in the first place? "They're actually missing the thing even from their own language": they say "the laws of nature", and a law means somebody is making this law. Where does it come from? What is the root of the *muskal* (the concept)?

Delving into the root reaches where the whole spring of *chachma* comes from: the depths of *chachma*, *taalumos chachma*, its hidden parts. As *bina*, called *yesh*, has depth, length and width, so does the spring of *chachma*, called *ayin*.

blocks.title: One aquifer under Pittsburgh and California
blocks.text: The depth of the spring is the beginning of its source, deep down. Under the ground is the aquifer, "a giant ocean under the ground that the spring comes from". One spring and another spring both connect to the same *taalumos chachma*: follow physics or psychology to their ultimate conclusion and they come from the same source. On the surface they are two things, "this one is in Pittsburgh, that one's in California. But when you go down far enough, you see there's really one big ocean down there that they're both coming from."

The spring that bursts out drop by drop from its hiddenness is the external spring. As in "the wellsprings of the deep burst open": what we call the spring "is really the tail of the spring", like its *Malchus*, not its *Keser*. The earth has veins, fissures, the same as with oil, and they have a first depth: the springs you see out here are not the real *mahus* (what it is in itself) of the spring; what makes it is the first depth, the aquifer. Of this it says, "*Chachma* is found from *ayin*": from the hiddenness of *chachma*, called the depth of *chachma*.

phrases.he: והחכמה הוא המצאת שכל החדש שיוצא כברק
phrases.en: It's a discovery of a new idea which comes out like a lightning.

phrases.he: כו' כידוע,
ומקור מחצבו
phrases.en: But the actual root of it, the source of it,

phrases.he: בהעלם עומקו הוא עיקר עצמיות ותוך תוכו
phrases.en: That's the real *atzmiyus* of the *chachma*.

blocks.text:
"*Chachma* is found from *ayin*": *chachma* is already a *metzius* (an existence); its real *ayin* is *taalumos chachma*. Then the definition: *chachma* is the discovery of a new idea that comes out like lightning.

But the lightning is already *Yesod Abba*. Even in revealed *chachma*, the flash is already the *yesh* of *chachma*: *Yesod* is the connection to the outside, where the idea can be brought into an actual *yesh*. When somebody has a new thought, the *bina* brings it out from this flash.

So two things: *chachma* is a new idea that comes out like lightning, but its source, hidden in its depth, is its real selfness, *taalumos chachma* in the *Keser*. That is why Kabbalistic and Chassidic books sometimes say *chachma* and mean revealed *chachma*, and often mean the *chachma* of *Arich*. When it says the Torah comes from *chachma*, it means the *chachma* of *Arich*, not the revealed *chachma* of *Atzilus*.

sections.title: The depth of the concept is a tamtzis, and yet it is the fiftieth gate
sections.summary: The depth of the concept in *bina* is only the *tamtzis* of an explanation, the *ayin* of its *yesh*, like instant coffee from the beans. Yet it is the *shaar hanun*, whose root reaches the depths of *chachma*: delving into it brings new light into the same book, and, unlike a bare flash, holds that light as a *yesh* that can be explained.

phrases.he: כנ"ל בביאור ענין עומק המושג דבינה
שאינ' רק העומק של ההשגה דבינה המורגש בבחינת יש בהבנת דבר מה בסברא נגלית,
phrases.en: The *omek hamusag* is the depth of the explanation, that's felt in an actual way of a somethingness when you understand something in the *sevara niglis*.

phrases.he: שעומק של הסבר ההשגה הוא בחינת אין של היש דהשגה בלבד,
phrases.en: When you understand the explanation, it's in a way of an *ayin*, but it's only the *ayin* of the *yesh* of this explanation.

phrases.he: ואין לו ערך לגבי אין דחכמה
טרם שבא לכלל השגה כלל,
phrases.en: Where the *chachma* is still not in a way of this particular explanation altogether.

phrases.he: גם לא בבחינת העומק שבה,
שהוא תמציתה
phrases.en: This *omek hamusag* is the *tamtzis*. The *tamtzis* means the essence.

blocks.text: Now *bina* is a *mashal* for *chachma*. The *omek hamusag* is the depth of the explanation, felt as a somethingness when you understand something in a revealed *sevara*; a *sevara* is already a *yesh*, like a theory. Understanding the explanation is an *ayin*, but only the *ayin* of the *yesh* of this explanation. It has no comparison to the *ayin* of *chachma* before it comes into comprehension at all, not yet in this particular explanation.

He is explaining *chachma* here, with *bina* as the *mashal*. The *omek hamusag* is the *ayin* of the *yesh*; the flash is the *yesh* of the *ayin*. Deeper is the *ayin* of the *ayin*, and deeper still the total *ayin* of *taalumos chachma*, which has nothing to do with this particular *chachma*. All the wisdoms come from it: not just this spring, all the springs.

Its *tamtzis* (essence): the *omek hamusag* is the *tamtzis*, the essence, like essence of almond. ("In English, somehow they use essence for self.") Why *davka* this term? A *tamtzis* is a derivative: what is left after you've processed the thing and come to its ultimate conclusion. After you process the whole explanation you come to its *tamtzis*, and now you understand it, like addition.

blocks.question: So how do you translate *Atzmus*?
blocks.text: Selfness. "It's always mistranslated": they call it "quintessential", "a very bad mistranslation". Essence means *tamtzis*: you processed the whole thing and got the taste out of it.

blocks.title: Instant coffee, and knowing how to add
blocks.text: Instant coffee is the *tamtzis* of coffee beans: you got out just the part you need. Or addition. Little kids are told one fishy plus one fishy is two fishies; by second or third grade it's one plus one is two, a whole bunch of examples, homework. Finally I know how to add. Which example? All of them. "Do I have a fantastic computer in my brain that has every single number addition in it, like 2,500 plus 7,600? No, I just have the *tamtzis* of the whole thing." I threw away the examples I had to sit and do and kept the way to add. That *tamtzis* is the *omek hamusag*: what you have when you went through the whole explanation.

blocks.title: "She thinks there's a G-d in the world; I know it"
blocks.text:
There is a summary before the *hisbonenus* and a summary after (he thinks it's in *Kuntres HaHispaalus*). The one before is: there's a G-d in the world.

The Deitschel (some say the Alter Rebbe, with his father-in-law) was asked, "So what did you learn?" "I learned there's a G-d in the world." "Hey, the maid knows that." He called the maid: "Do you know there's a G-d in the world?" "Sure, who does not know there's a G-d in the world?" He answered: "She thinks there's a G-d in the world. I know there's a G-d in the world."

He had the summary after the *hisbonenus*; she had the one before. Here again is where they make their mistake: on the surface the two look exactly the same. He said what the maid said. "So what's the difference? What makes him the big Rebbe and she's just a stupid maid?" He had the *tamtzis* afterwards, and, as he will explain, there is more even after the *tamtzis*. That is the *omek hamusag*.

blocks.text: Yet the depth of the concept is called the *shaar hanun* (fiftieth gate) of *bina*. "But wait a minute, there's another *omek hamusag*." The *shaar hanun* is not so simple: even Moshe Rabbeinu had a hard time getting to it. So how can it be just the *tamtzis* of the explanation? There is depth, and there is depth of the depth.

blocks.title: The locust's antenna, the shofar and the horn of plenty
blocks.text: Even though it is drawn from the *ayin* of *chachma* to the *yesh* of an explanation, it is like the spring that comes out of the Holy of Holies, which starts off like the antenna of a locust. That is why *bina* is called a shofar: narrow at the start, wide at the end. And the horn of plenty, the cornucopia: narrow on one side, open on the other.

Its root reaches into the depth of *chachma*. The first depth is the *Keser* of *bina* of *Atzilus*. But as *chachma* has its depth in the *chachma* of *Arich*, there is also a *bina* of *Arich*; and the *shaar hanun* keeps going higher, to the *bina* of *Atik*, and into *Radla*. As he explains later, "we will rejoice and be glad in You, *mamash*", in a way higher even than *chachma*. That is the Leviathan, who can jump from the upper waters to the lower and from the lower to the upper.

We see it plainly: whoever delves just into the depth of the concept finds its root. We are delving into the explanation of *Shaar HaYichud*: the first chapters explain what *hisbonenus* is, and from chapter 10 he explains how the world came into existence, the *seder hishtalshelus* (the chain of worlds), not G-d. Nonetheless it brings out new light of *chachma* in *bina*.

blocks.title: Every time, a whole new book
blocks.text: Concentrating only on the *omek hamusag*, the explanation, still brings new light of *chachma* into the *bina*. Shimon often says that each time he reads the book, it's a whole new book. "It's the same book with exactly the same letters. The book didn't change." But now he sees it in a new light of *chachma* in the *bina*, though each time he only learned the explanation. And some of what we talk about is not even explained in the book. "Where did we get them? We got them from the book."

That is why it is called *ma'amik*. *Omek hadaas* (depth of *daas*) is concentrating while you learn, as we are doing now. Later, after we finish, we'll be walking around thinking about it: what does it really mean, what is its root? *Ma'amik* is a causative form, "activation": it activates the depth of *chachma* and *bina*, in *Arich*, then in *Atik*, and even more.

He doesn't know if the text says this later, but *bina* has an advantage over *chachma*. The *shaar hanun* is a *yesh*, yet when it reaches into the depth of *chachma* it grabs it as a *yesh*, so he can bring it out into an explanation and to other people. Someone who just gets a spiritual insight, an intuitive feeling, can't explain it to somebody else and may even lose it himself: a few days later "it dissipates."

Like people who get real drunk, or stoned, and have a flash of wisdom, and the next day don't remember it at all. Or the story about Edison and others: if they didn't write a flash of *chachma* down right away, they would *mamash* lose it. The *shaar hanun* of *bina* goes just as deep as *chachma*, but gets it as a *yesh*.

sections.title: Wise in understanding, understanding in wisdom: the inventor and the navon
sections.summary: "Be wise in understanding" is *chachma sheb'bina*: a new insight, but only in the same field, and it comes only through the *iyun* of *bina sheb'bina*, held in the *kli* of *daas*; go for *chiddushim* and you make none. "Understand with wisdom" is *bina sheb'chachma*: the power to explain an insight many ways, and, deeper, the *navon* who understands one thing from another, even a different field, because he has reached the aquifer.

שמבואר בכתבים, דהיינו ע''ב דס''ג חכם בבינה,
phrases.en: *Chacham babina* means *chachma* of *bina*.

phrases.he: שהוא רק להבין דבר חידוש אחר מתוך המושג דבינה,
phrases.en: To understand just a new *chiddush*, but in this same *bina*.

שהוא המברר כל חלקיו על בוריו,
phrases.en: The *iyun* means analysis: to separate out all the parts of it according to its various classifications.

phrases.en: And this analysis of the thing into its parts is called *bina sheb'bina*.

blocks.text: "Understand with wisdom, and be wise in understanding." "Wise in understanding" is *chachma* of *bina*: only to understand another new thing from the concept of *bina*, a new *chiddush* (insight), but in this same *bina*.

blocks.title: Not from the Himalayas
blocks.text: An innovation in computers "is not made by somebody who went in the Himalayas and meditated". It's made *davka* by the people who work with computers over and over and think about it. About what? Not the innovation; they didn't know it. They thought about what they already know, and came up with an innovation.

blocks.title: From the Model T to the Pentium 4
blocks.text: Cars keep getting better; a car now is not a Model T from the 1930s. Who came up with it? The engineers at the car companies. Where did a guy learn about cars? In college, about the cars we already have. An engineer, in waterworks or electricity, or a doctor, learns *davka* what we already know, not what he will invent. Yet he invents, and *davka* in his field: an engineer in computers is not going to invent a new drug that will cure certain diseases; he's going to invent a better computer. The Pentium, the Pentium II, III, 4, and soon a computer you just talk to, without a keyboard. How do they get better and better? That is *chachma sheb'bina*.

Going over the *bina sheb'bina*, this and this again, is the activating power of all the other powers; later he will explain that the activation of the lower powers, the *middos* (emotional attributes), also comes *davka* from *bina sheb'bina*. And it has to work within the *kli* of *daas*.

blocks.title: The would-be millionaire
blocks.text: Somebody wants to be a computer genius but isn't interested in computers. Why, then? "Well, I want to make computer inventions, and then I'll be a millionaire." "He's probably not going to invent nothing new." He goes to college and learns the information, not the subject: he does the *bina sheb'bina* without the *kli* of *daas*.

blocks.title: A glass with no water, water with no glass
blocks.text: *Daas* is not totally nothing: it's a necessary *kli*, like a glass of water. Without the glass the water spills. Give a guy dying of thirst in the desert a glass, "that's not going to help him nothing"; give him water without a glass and it spills in the sand: "Hey, oh you're thirsty? Here's some water." Without the *kli* the water is useless, and the *kli* by itself is also useless.

Only through the *iyun*. *Chachma sheb'bina* doesn't come by saying, "Okay, I'm going to innovate something now." The Rebbe Rashab's tract on how to learn Gemara says: don't go for *chiddushim*. If you try, your *chiddush* will be "a real *chiddush*": invented out of your head, not told to Moshe Rabbeinu on Mount Sinai. The actual *chiddush* of a seasoned student comes when you learn the text of the Gemara, then with Rashi. "What? Just Talmud with Rashi? How am I going to be an innovator?" "If you want to be an innovator, you'll never be an innovator." It is *davka* doing the *iyun* that brings the *chiddush* automatically.

So it is *davka* through the *iyun*, and that is what the whole chapter is about: *bina sheb'bina* within the *kli* of *daas* activates all the powers, above it or below it. *Kuntres HaHispaalus* explains that the *hispaalus* of the *middos* comes *davka* from *hisbonenus*; here, the higher powers too. You want the depth of *chachma*, the flash of light, the unification with the infinite light. "Oh, I'll meditate on the light." "No, it doesn't work like that."

The *iyun* activates the powers below it, and even *daas*. We have a bigger *daas* in this (not a knowledge *daas*, a connection to it) than someone who learned less, because we activated it up to the *Keser*. In anything: the more you understand about something, the more your *daas* toward it is activated.

There is also a negative *daas*. Understanding more about something, you may see it is bad, and get a *daas* to stay away from it, the opposite of concentration: you don't want to think about it at all. Either way, more understanding activates more *daas*.

blocks.title: Red, green and blue: sorting a thing into its parts
blocks.text: *Iyun* sorts out every part clearly: analysis, separating a thing into its classifications. "Okay, this one is the red one, you put it here, and this one is the green one, you put it here." Three red, two green, a blue one: that's how a television screen makes its picture. The same with everything. A personality is intellect and emotions: the first separation, into two. Intellect is *chachma*, *bina* and *daas*, with the super-intellect of *Keser* above. The emotions are seven, divided basically into love and hate, or love and fear, and within love there are ten more. You separate it more and more. This analysis of a thing into its parts is called *bina sheb'bina*.

phrases.he: ואחר כך
phrases.en: Only when he does this analysis,

phrases.he: יוכל להוליד ולהתחכם להמציא הבנה והשגה חדשה,
אבל רק בהשגה זו עצמה
phrases.en: Just to make an innovation in this *hasaga* itself,

phrases.he: שנקרא חכמה שבבינה,
אבל כתר דבינה הוא עומק המושג הנזכר לעיל,
המגיע שרשו בעומק החכמה כנזכר לעיל.
phrases.en: But the *shoresh* of the *Keser* of *bina* is in *omek hachachma*.

blocks.text: Only after this analysis can he give birth, be wise, and come up with a new understanding. *Davka* someone who knows every part of a car can make a better car. "I could not come up with a better car, because I have no idea how the motor works." Someone who knows every single part of the motor can come up with a better motor.

But only in this comprehension itself: only in a car; he can't innovate outside his field. "Well, what about the Wright brothers?" It's still a traveling machine: they took a motor from a car and put it on the airplane. Going from one field to another is in a way *tevuna*, also an innovation, of *bina sheb'chachma*. *Chachma sheb'bina* is just to innovate in this *hasaga* itself.

But the *Keser* of *bina* is the depth of the concept. It too has an outer side, just understanding the explanation, but its root is in the depth of *chachma*: what he really wants to understand is not the explanation but the actual thing. That is what *chachma sheb'bina* is.

phrases.he: והבן בחכמה
phrases.en: *V'havein bechachma* means *bina* of *chachma*.

phrases.he: היינו ס''ג דע''ב, שהוא כח ההסבר בחכמה עצמה,
phrases.en: The *hiyuli*, inherent power of explanation within a *chachma*.

phrases.he: שיוכל להביאו בפנים מסבירות הרבה,
phrases.en: You'll be able to explain it in different ways, not just in one way.

phrases.he: והוא למעלה מן ההשגה דבינה עדיין
phrases.en: But this is still higher than the actual *hasaga*.

blocks.text: "Understand with wisdom" is *bina* of *chachma*, *SaG* of *Ayin Beis*: the power of explanation within *chachma* itself, its *hiyuli* (raw potential). When you grasp a thing beyond the explanation, as the *ayin* of *chachma*, you haven't explained it yet, but if somebody asks, you can explain it, and in many different ways. That is still above the comprehension of *bina*: not an explanation, "a *hiyuli* for explanation".

phrases.he: ומה שאמרו נבונים לא אשתכחו,
phrases.en: But what they said,

phrases.he: שהוא המבין דבר מתוך דבר דוקא
phrases.en: To understand a deeper wisdom from an external wisdom.

phrases.he: היינו מצד שרש כח זה דהבן בחכמה שמגיע בעומק דחכמה הנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: The inner power of *bina* of *chachma* reaches, like we said, into the aquifer,

phrases.he: על כן יוכל להבין דבר חכמה אחרת לגמרי מתוך דבר חכמה זאת
phrases.en: and that's why he can understand a different *chachma* from this *chachma*.

blocks.text: "Men of understanding were not to be found" is something besides the power of explanation: *bina sheb'chachma* has two things. The power of explanation goes downwards, bringing *chachma* into explanations of *bina*. But the "and" here means "but": they didn't mean there is nobody who could explain it. That's something... (the side of the tape ends here).

Therefore he can understand an altogether different wisdom from this one: the inner power of *bina* of *chachma* reaches into the depth of *chachma*, the aquifer.

So *bina* of *chachma* is really three things. Going downwards, it is the inherent power to bring a *chachma* out into an explanation. Its real, inner thing is to understand one thing from another, a deeper wisdom from an external one. And because he goes into the aquifer, the source of all the wisdoms, he can carry it from this field into a different field altogether. "It can go down, it can go up, and it can go sideways."

blocks.title: The Wright brothers' bicycle chain
blocks.text: It's a width: he brings it into a different wisdom, which can be on the same level. Like the Wright brothers, bicycle makers interested in cars, who brought it into airplanes. ("They were not really total *navonim*", but it's good for an external *mashal*.) They didn't look at a motor as a car motor; they looked into its root, a supplier of power: if it can power a car, it can power an airplane. And as bicycle makers they knew the chains and the gears with teeth that connect into them; the original airplanes had those connecting to the propeller. "So they took from bicycles to airplanes."

Why? Someone on a more external level knows how to make a bicycle and never thinks how a chain applies to anything else. They thought into its root: not a bicycle, but a way to move the energy from the feet to the wheel through the chain and the gear. They saw the inner point: a way to move energy from one thing to another.

phrases.he: שזהו למעלה במדריגה מן החכם,
phrases.en: A *navon* is higher than a *chacham*.

phrases.he: דהיינו מגופה של המצאות החכמה זו מאין,
שאינו מבין ממנה חכמה ושכל אחר

blocks.text: This is higher in level even than the wise man. Explaining outwards, *bina sheb'chachma* is lower than *chachma sheb'chachma*; but its inner level, the *navon*, is higher than the *chacham*, who is *chachma sheb'chachma* and just has an invention. The *navon* may not come up with a new invention, but takes an old invention and comes up with a whole new thing. It has a higher source, reaching deeper than *chachma* itself: understanding one thing from another.

Remember, this is about what *hisbonenus* is in *Chassidus*. Understanding one thing from another is the power of *bina sheb'chachma* behind "we will rejoice and be glad in You, *mamash*", later. *Bina sheb'bina* activates *chachma sheb'bina*, which activates *bina sheb'chachma*. Then, with *chachma* itself, seeing as with an eye, from the *seder hishtalshelus* he understands what is deeper than the *seder hishtalshelus*.

phrases.he: (ומכל מקום מה שבהשגה דבינה מבין השגה חדשה מתוך ההשגה זו, שרשה בהבן דחכמה,
phrases.en: The *shoresh* of *chachma sheb'bina* is in *bina sheb'chachma*.

phrases.he: שמבין דבר מתוך דבר,
רק שזה בהעלם מקור השכל
phrases.en: Except that one of them is in the hidden part of the *sechel*, and the other one is in the revealed part of the *sechel*.

phrases.he: כו' ודי למבין).

blocks.text: Still, when *bina* understands a new comprehension from this one, that has its root in the "understanding" of *chachma*: the root of *chachma sheb'bina* is *bina sheb'chachma*. Only one is in the hidden part of the intellect, the other in the revealed part.

sections.title: The order of the levels, and the student's way: up the length to the depth
sections.summary: *Hisbonenus* starts with *bina sheb'bina*, which gives a concept its length; *chachma sheb'bina* gives it width; and how long and wide it gets depends on its depth, the *Keser* of *bina*. The main point, which the text leaves unsaid, runs the other way: the student reaches the depth only by going up one length at a time, the way Moshiach will split the river.

phrases.he: ונמצא סדר המדרגות כך הם,
בחינת עיון הנזכר לעיל
לעמוד על בוריו כו'
phrases.en: To go through the analysis of all the separate parts.

phrases.he: נקרא בינה שבבינה,
להבחין תכלית ההבחנה בפנימיות וחיצוניות
phrases.en: To examine to the utmost of examination the inner and outer things of whatever it is that you're examining.

blocks.text: So the order of the levels, how you do *hisbonenus*. You start with *bina sheb'bina*, the *iyun*: going through the analysis of all the separate parts, "to examine to the utmost of examination" the inner and the outer of whatever you are examining.

phrases.he: וגם מזה יוכל להיות בחינת האורך,
phrases.en: And also from this can come the *orech* of *bina*,

phrases.he: להוריד ההשגה בלבושים רבים עד שתתגשם להשגות התינוק כנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: meaning to explain it down into *meshalim*,

phrases.he: אבל לא בחינת הרוחב בהסברים שונים לכל צד כו'

blocks.text: From this can also come the length of *bina*: bringing it down in *meshalim* until a child can grasp it. But not the width, different explanations to every side: that is already an innovation. *Bina sheb'bina* understands within this explanation, only along its length.

phrases.he: ואחר כך מבחינת חכמה שבבינה,
להמציא חדשות
בהשגה א' כנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: But *davka* in this *hasaga*.

phrases.he: הוא הנקרא רוחב,
וממנו כח דבינה שבבינה העושה בחינת אורך

blocks.text: Then *chachma sheb'bina*, coming up with new things, but *davka* in this one comprehension, is called width: a new twist on the thing. And from it the power of *bina sheb'bina* makes length: when you understand a new twist and analyze it, you can make a whole new length.

phrases.he: אבל שיעור האורך והרוחב דחכמה ובינה שבבינה, הוא תלוי בבחינת עומק המושג שנקרא כתר דבינה,
phrases.en: According to the *omek hamusag* of a certain thing, that's how much length and width you're going to have.

phrases.he: וכנראה בחוש שלפי ערך העומק כך יהיה ערך הרוחב והאורך בכל השגת דבר מה
phrases.en: In any kind of thing, according to how deep the subject matter is, that's how much length and width there will be in it.

phrases.he: וד"ל).

blocks.title: Chess and checkers
blocks.text: But the measure of the length and width depends on the depth of the concept, the *Keser* of *bina*. In *Chassidus*, what we're learning here, the length and width can be fantastic because the depth is fantastic. Chess has a bigger width and length than checkers; everybody understands it's a deeper game, so there are all kinds of books of chess strategy. "In checkers you can also write, but how much can you write already?" Not like chess: its depth is bigger.

blocks.title: The doctor who went through the length
blocks.text: It also works vice versa: you don't get to the depth by concentrating on it, only *davka* by going through the length and the width. A doctor who learned for seven years knows more about medicine than a layman: all the explanations, where all the bones and organs are. When *Chassidus* talks about the liver, or how the brain is made, a doctor can explain the physical makeup. Why? Because a doctor went through the length.

A doctor who knows not only occidental medicine but oriental, homeopathic and other kinds has a width, and might be a better doctor than one who knows only one explanation. Because he has a bigger width, he might have a bigger depth also. It works both ways.

sensitivity.reason: Suggests a doctor who also knows oriental and homeopathic medicine may be the better doctor.
sensitivity.publishable: Someone who knows a field in more than one way has a width, and because he has a bigger width he might have a bigger depth also. So it works both ways.

blocks.text: The *omek hamusag* of a thing sets how much length and width it will have, and vice versa: how far you get into the depth depends *davka* on how much you went through the length and the width. We see plainly that as deep as a subject is, so is its length and width, "and basically really, it's also the other way around."

He doesn't say it here, but the real main point of this chapter is the reverse: reaching into the depth depends on how much you went through the length and width, *davka* through the *bina sheb'bina*, really through the length, "because you shouldn't make *chiddushim*." He said it from up to down, depth to width to length, as a teacher teaches it. But we go from down up: the student should concentrate *davka* on the length.

Concentrate on a width and you get nothing; you just jump around. One day it's physics, he wants to be a physicist. The next day, "Yeah, you know what? I want to be a chemist." Then computers. Then, "No, I want to make airplanes." As he says later, someone with a wide *daas* and no deep *daas* "really doesn't have a *daas* at all": it's all spread. They know about baseball, football, a little bit about this, "but there's nothing that they're really into", so ultimately they don't know too much about anything: no deep *daas* in one thing that really turns them on.

*Daas* has to hold you onto the length. A width is multiple lengths, and to learn you do *davka* *bina sheb'bina*, a single length. People who learned various Kabbalistic stuff read here and say, "What do you mean? *Chachma* is this? It says *chachma* is not this." That's a different length. To learn this length, forget that one; try to put them together and you're not ready for the width, until you go through the length. Go through the length of *Shaar HaYichud*, and then you'll understand how *chachma* has letters and doesn't, is a point and has dimensions: two aspects, two lengths, which together give a width. So it goes *davka* from *bina sheb'bina*: sit and learn a length, and forget about the other length.

From that comes *chachma sheb'bina*: you start seeing new things, *davka* in this explanation. Then the power of *bina sheb'chachma*, its outer side: the *hiyuli* of many different explanations. That activates *chachma sheb'chachma*, and that activates *bina sheb'chachma* going up into *taalumos chachma*: understanding one thing from another.

By the way, the river here is not about a river: going from the *mashal* to the *nimshal* (what it stands for) is itself *bina sheb'chachma*. And length here is not a physical length like a river's: going from down to up, it is understanding a thing from inside a thing, along the length.

blocks.title: Moshiach will split the river lengthwise
blocks.text: It says that when Moshiach comes he will open up the river. Moshe Rabbeinu opened up the sea; Moshiach will open the river, "lengthwise, not sideways": it says explicitly that he'll split it into seven streams, along the length. Then you'll go up the length into the depth. Take a boat up the river and you end up at the source, the spring; keep going and you end up in the aquifer. He'll open it all the way to the aquifer, so the wellsprings of the deep come out. That's the Flood: the hidden aquifer bursting into the revealed, with the lower depths and with the upper depths, also hidden, when the windows of heaven are opened. Now it's a window; he'll open it totally, like a ceiling with a little hole in it, and then the whole ceiling breaks down and all the water on top floods everything. "So that's what we're going to expect very soon."

blocks.question: Why does he mention *Ayin Beis* of *SaG* and *SaG* of *Ayin Beis* here, when the explanation would be exactly the same without them?
blocks.text: Right now the best thing is to skip it. "If you don't skip the whole thing, you'll just be stuck with it and you won't understand nothing." Later, maybe in chapter 12 (he doesn't remember which), he speaks of the yud of the *SaG*, and then we'll start understanding it. Partly, in his days it was written for kabbalists. And the whole matter of the Names, how this Name goes into *Ayin Beis*, *SaG* and the rest: now we have only a vague idea of what each letter means, and later we'll understand why he said it. "It's not for nothing." It's there for later; for now it's enough to understand *chachma* of *bina* and *bina* of *chachma*.

This is why we want so much to turn everybody else onto this: we're on "a 007 thing, actually since we're in the sixth millennium we're a 006 thing", a need-to-know basis. So it was by the prophets: when the *Aibershter* (G-d) was angry at the Jews, Moshe Rabbeinu didn't get prophecy. When other people learn and start asking this question, we'll have to know the answer, and then we'll know it. Then we'll sit in our retreat in the Catskills, or on the Golan Heights, with a whole yeshiva and all the books, and look up in *Etz Chaim* the *Ayin Beis* of the *SaG* and the *SaG* of the *Ayin Beis*, what the yud means, and why in *Ayin Beis* the vav is spelled vav-yud-vav and in *SaG* vav-alef-vav. "And then we'll understand."

For now the answer is that this book was written for kabbalists. That's why Rabbi Markel mostly tells people not to learn the Reb Hillel Paritcher: it is more complicated than this and brings in a lot more Kabbala. Part of what Reb Hillel is doing is answering the complaint people had against the Mitteler Rebbe, as against the *Rambam*: he didn't bring sources. "Where is he coming up with this crazy stuff from? That's not what it says in *Etz Chaim*." *Etz Chaim* says *Ayin Beis* of *SaG*, and he's talking about something you can apply to building cars and bicycles. "Hey, told you that's the *Ayin Beis* of the *SaG* and the *SaG* of the *Ayin Beis*." So Reb Hillel Paritcher is a lot of apologetics, "not exactly apologetics", showing how this comes from Kabbala, and for that you have to know the Kabbala.

blocks.text: At the level we're holding, that's the best explanation. This book is like a Torah scroll. The story of Yosef and his brothers is a story for little kids ("so therefore you should treat your brother nicely"), it's on the level of a big rabbi in halacha, and of the biggest kabbalist, the *Arizal*. This book too: "even a brand new guy who doesn't know from nothing" can sit with it and learn it.

blocks.title: What the Rebbe Rashab was proudest of
blocks.text: What was the Rebbe Rashab most proud of in the Frierdiker Rebbe? You'd think many things. It was that he read the *Shaar HaYichud* without his father telling him to, and wrote a commentary on it. Rabbi Markel doesn't think they read this book the way we are reading it. It is written on every level.

When the *Aibershter* decided to be the *Aibershter*, He had to read this book to find out who He is. Then Jackie Mason: "I went to a psychologist. He says, I'm going to help you find yourself. What do you mean find myself? I'm right over here! I know where I am! He says, no, I'm going to help you find out who you are. You mean I'm not me? I thought I was me. So maybe really you're me and I'm you, so you give me the 50 bucks!"

sensitivity.reason: Jokes that G-d had to read this book to find out who He is; it sets up the identity-crisis joke of the next block.
sensitivity.publishable: Another story, with Jackie Mason: "I went to a psychologist. He says, I'm going to help you find yourself. What do you mean find myself? I'm right over here! I know where I am! He says, no, I'm going to help you find out who you are. You mean I'm not me? I thought I was me. So maybe really you're me and I'm you, so you give me the 50 bucks!"

blocks.text: So when the *Aibershter* had an identity crisis and wanted to find out who He is, all He had to do was read the *Shaar HaYichud*. "I know it sounds kind of funny", but it's *mamash* written even for the *Aibershter*. That's why He wanted the world: "he wanted to get the explanation *davka* from idiots, the way that we understand it." Today's three-way conference call was actually four-way: one line was arranged for the *Aibershter*, listening in. He found out a whole bunch of things: "Oh, so that's who I am, maybe you'll give me the 50 bucks."

sensitivity.publishable: So this book is written even, as it were, for the *Aibershter*. That's why He wanted the world: to get the explanation *davka* from us, the way we understand it. Today's three-way conference call was actually a four-way conference call: one line was arranged for the *Aibershter*, and He was listening in too.

sections.title: Daas is the dive, not the depth: the bond that holds a concept
sections.summary: Concentration is not the depth of a concept but what carries one to it, as a dive carries a diver to the ocean floor; and it works only after the *iyun* has given it the explanation. *Daas* has length (attention span, holding a long idea), width and depth, and its depth, as with the boy who loved hockey, draws out its length.

phrases.he: ולפ"ז
phrases.en: So according to what we said before,

phrases.he: מה שקוראים העולם העמקת הדעת,
אין זה גופה של העמקה,
phrases.en: That's not the actual essence of the depth. It's not the actual body of the depth.

phrases.he: כמו עומק המושג דבינה,
phrases.en: Like for instance the *omek hamusag d'bina*, which means the actual depth of the actual concept,

phrases.he: שלזה לא יש שייכות לדעת
phrases.en: This has nothing to do with concentration.

blocks.title: The dive and the floor of the ocean
blocks.text: So much for *chachma* and *bina*; now *daas*. What the world calls *ha'amakas hadaas* (concentration) is not the body of the depth itself: it is the deepening, not the depth. Take a deep dive off a board: concentration is the dive, the depth is the pool you're going to. Or in Hawaii, where they throw money off the boat and those guys jump off their little boats and go down to get it: "the depth is the floor of the ocean", and concentration "is the dive that gets them there."

Such as the depth of the concept in *bina*, the actual depth of the actual concept, which has nothing to do with *daas*. To understand how computers work you have to concentrate in school, but the *omek hamusag* itself has nothing to do with concentration.

phrases.he: אך הדעת הוא בחינת התקשרות הרגשתו במושג ביותר,
phrases.en: Concentration, in other words: to connect your feeling into the *musag* very much.

phrases.he: והוא שמביא לידי בחינת העמקה במושג, אחר בחינת העיון הנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: And this is what brings a man to going deeply into the *musag*, after the analysis.

phrases.he: שהוא רק כמו בחינת כלי לעומק ההשגה כנזכר לעיל.
phrases.en: The *daas* is only a *kli* to get deeply into the *hasaga*, but you have to have the *hasaga*.

phrases.he: וגם בדעת יש אורך ורוחב ועומק,
כמו יש מי שדעתו קצרה
phrases.en: Like there's somebody who has a very short *daas*, meaning the attention span.

phrases.he: ויש שדעתו ארוכה
phrases.en: So there's some people that have a much longer attention span; they can sit with one thing for a much longer time.

phrases.he: ויש שדעתו רחבה ולא ארוכה
phrases.en: He knows a little bit of everything, but he can't stay with one thing for a long time.

phrases.he: ודעת חזק
phrases.en: Or else a very strong *daas*, which means he's very opinionated.

phrases.he: או דעת קל
phrases.en: Meaning that it's very easy to change his opinion.

phrases.he: כנשים שדעתן קלות,
phrases.en: In women:

phrases.he: הוא בלתי עומק הדעת וממילא דעתו קצרה כו'
phrases.en: And since he's not very deeply into the thing, therefore his *daas* is also short.

blocks.text: Rather, *daas* is connecting one's feeling into the concept very much: concentration. It brings one to delve into the concept after the *iyun*: knowing all the details is not enough. Two kids sit in a classroom, one getting A's and one getting D's. They heard exactly the same explanation from the same teacher, but in one there was *daas* and in the other none, so one got to the *omek hamusag* and one didn't.

Still, only after the *iyun*. If a kid says, "Since I concentrate so hard, I'll just stay home and concentrate," it won't work: he didn't get the explanation. *Daas* is only a *kli* to get deeply into the *hasaga*, "but you have to have the *hasaga*."

***Daas* too has length, width and depth**: **there is one whose *daas* is short**: the attention span, long or short, one of the things in learning *Chassidus*. Both of these books, like *Ayin Beis*, are a *hemshech* (a continuous series of discourses). That means that for the proper *hisbonenus* of the *daas*, once you have the *omek hamusag*, you have to hold the entire book in your head at one shot, or at least a part of it: chapter one, or this little paragraph about *daas* we're learning now. That is one side of the length of *daas*.

The other side: how long can you concentrate? "If you have an attention span of three seconds, I won't be able to learn with you": after three seconds you're somewhere else. Our classes need an attention span of half an hour to an hour: a *daas* to leave everything and put your whole *daas* into just the class.

They did research: the maximum attention span of an American is about ten to fifteen minutes; that's why TV has the commercials. In movies too, a scene that runs too long loses the audience. "Those long, long, drawn Indian movies, an American won't be able to sit through it." Or some of these artsy Scandinavian movies.

sensitivity.reason: Generalises about Americans' attention span and pokes fun at Indian and Scandinavian films.
sensitivity.publishable: Research says a television audience's attention span is about ten to fifteen minutes; that's why they put the commercials. In movies too, a scene that runs too long loses the audience.

blocks.text: So a short *daas* is a short attention span, and also how long you can hold on to an idea. In *Ayin Beis* one idea can run 50, 60, 100 chapters; after a while you don't know what he's talking about anymore, because holding ten chapters "your mind is already blowing up". You need an incredible length of *daas*: some ideas are 30 to 100 chapters long, and really the whole thing is one idea. Rabbi Markel knows he has a longer *daas* than most, "because I have the *daas* from here", and still sometimes can't hold part of an idea 30 chapters long: "After a while I have no idea what he's talking. I forget what he was talking about before. I can't hold a whole thing in my mind because my *daas* is not that long."

one whose *daas* is long: some can sit with one thing much longer (kids, you notice, have a very short attention span). one whose *daas* is wide but not long: a little bit of everything, but nothing for long. a strong *daas*: very opinionated. or a light *daas*: it's very easy to change his opinion.

like women, whose *daas* is light. It doesn't mean some women don't have a stronger *daas* than certain men. Take a frum woman who is into learning: if she says, "What do you mean I have a light *daas*?", most men don't have as heavy a *daas* as she does; she is not like some guy into rock and roll. But "we're talking in terms of people who are on the same level": look at that guy's girlfriend and her *daas* is even lighter than his. Or the wife of one of the great rabbis: "Look at her, she has a bigger *daas* than you did." "Yeah, but if you look at her in comparison to her husband, it might not be like that. It's according to the level."

sensitivity.reason: Compares the daas of women and men in his own examples beyond the line's words.
sensitivity.publishable: **like women, whose *daas* is light**. It doesn't mean there aren't some women who have a stronger *daas* than certain men; we're talking about people on the same level. It's according to the level.

blocks.text: What does a light *daas* mean? Without depth of *daas*, and so the *daas* is short, like a little kid's: not being deeply into the thing, his *daas* is short. As with *bina*, the depth brings about the width and the length.

blocks.title: The boy who loved hockey
blocks.text: If somebody is really deep into a thing, it changes. Rabbi Markel knew a kid who looked like he had no *daas* at all, no attention span for nothing in school. But he loved hockey. His hockey books had whole pages of statistics, "like a whole mathematical book"; in mathematics he was doing lousy, but the statistics of who shot and how many points he scored he could sit with for hours. The depth of *daas* you have in something makes the length longer.

phrases.he: והפרש זה בין קלי הדעת לעומקי הדעת,
phrases.en: When people have a light *daas*, and people who have a deep *daas*:

phrases.he: בין גדול לקטן ידוע,
phrases.en: it's the same thing like an older person and a younger person.

phrases.he: שהתינוק שדעתו קל,
phrases.en: A *tinok* has a light *daas*,

phrases.he: היינו שאין בו כח המרגיש והתקשרות כלל לדבר זה שמבין או רוצה בו, רק בחיצוניות מאד
phrases.en: he doesn't have such a strong, real feeling or *hiskashrus* to this thing, only in a very external way.

phrases.he: על כן יתפתה להיפוכו,
מה שאין כן הגדול שדעתו עמוקה באותו דבר שמבין או רוצה בו,
הוא הנקרא העמקת הדעת,
phrases.en: That's called *omek hadaas*: the connection to the thing.

phrases.he: שממילא נמשך אורך הדעת ורוחב הדעת כנזכר לעיל בבינה.
phrases.en: Somebody who is really into the thing deeply, automatically he'll have the long attention span and he'll be able to hold long ideas in his head, and also be able to have the *rochav* of seeing it in many different ways; like it said in *bina*.

blocks.text: The difference between light and deep *daas* is known, as between an adult and a child: a child's *daas* is light, with no real feeling or connection to what he understands or wants, **only in a very external way**.

So a kid wants and wants this toy, you get it for him, and "two seconds later he's already forgot about it", because the connection was only external; it never touched him on an inner level. An adult whose *daas* is deep in what he understands or wants, "like a communist or something like that", is connected in a much more inner way. That connection is *omek hadaas*, and from it automatically come the length and width of *daas*: the long attention span, holding long ideas, seeing it in many different ways. As in *bina*, the length and width come from the depth.

sections.title: Deep daas squeezes the whole mind into one point, and daas and bina depend on each other
sections.summary: The sign of deep *daas* is a face *farkvetsht* around one point, the opposite of *iyun*, which spreads into every detail; a class on *daas* thinks of nothing but *daas*. Point by point, that brings one to the root of the concept, up to *daas elyon*, which unites *chachma* and *bina*. *Daas* without *bina* is the *daas* of *Tohu*, and *bina* without *daas* is not learned.

phrases.he: וסימן להעמקת הדעת
phrases.en: The external *siman* that somebody is concentrating:

phrases.he: הוא אשר נראה כענין צמצום וכיווץ כלי המוח, לעוצם עומק התקשרותו במושכל,
phrases.en: It looks like he's *kvetching* up his brain as far as how deeply he is connected to the *muskal*.

phrases.he: (בל"א ער איז דרינן פר נומען פר קוועצט שטארק
phrases.en: He's really all taken up, and strongly *farkvetsht*,

phrases.he: זייער ביז עס3 איז זייער מצומצם
phrases.en: he's very *metzumtzam*,

phrases.he: רק בתנוע' אחת4 וסקירה אחת לבד כו')
phrases.en: in one movement and one look.

phrases.he: שמזה דוקא בא עצם עומק השגה על ידי העיון דבינה
phrases.en: *Davka* from this thing of getting totally *farkvetsht* into the one *inyan*.

blocks.text: The sign of *ha'amakas hadaas*, the external sign that somebody is concentrating: it looks like a contracting and squeezing of the vessel of the brain, as if he's kvetching up his brain, as deeply as he is connected to the concept.

blocks.title: Rabbi Raichik's nose through the tallis
blocks.text: Rabbi Raichik, may he rest in peace, had a long, sharp nose. Rabbi Markel saw him sometimes davening, concentrating so hard "that his nose would come out through the back of his tallis". That's the sign: you kvetch up your face, as if you're trying to kvetch up your brain.

sensitivity.reason: A joke about the nose of a named, recently deceased rabbi.
sensitivity.publishable: Rabbi Markel saw Rabbi Raichik, may he rest in peace, sometimes davening, concentrating very hard. That's the sign: you kvetch up your face, as if you're trying to kvetch up your brain.

blocks.text: In Yiddish: he is all taken up in it, *farkvetsht* strongly, until he is very contracted, in one movement and one look: totally focused on one thing, and outwardly his whole face gets *farkvetsht*.

From this *davka* comes the very depth of comprehension: getting totally *farkvetsht* into the one matter. The whole book is one *hemshech*, and finally the *iyun* needs the whole book in your head, but right now we're *farkvetsht* only into *daas*.

"This book is always a *mashal* on itself": whatever it talks about can be a *mashal* for what you're talking about. Right now we're *farkvetsht* about *daas*, not thinking about the *Malchus* of *tevuna*, how the letters or Leah come out, *chachma* and *bina*, or the crowns. If we did, "it would detract from our" delving into this.

Start discussing other things and you learn nothing. "A good student asks according to the matter." "Oh yeah, but what about the *Malchus* of *tevuna*?" "What are you talking about, *Malchus* of *tevuna*? We're talking about *daas*." "Yeah, okay, but what about the yud of the *SaG*, and what about this and what about that?" What brings the delving into the concept, the real *omek hamusag* we're learning, is *farkvetsht*-ing ourselves *davka* into this matter and leaving the others aside. through the *iyun* of *bina*: the *iyun* of *bina* cuts it up into little pieces, but now we go only into the one piece.

phrases.he: שהוא היפך הצמצום והכיווץ,
שהרי העיון דבינה, גם שעומד ומעוכב בצמצום וכיווץ בתחלתו,
אבל מיד מתפשת לרוחב הרבה בכל פרטי חלקיו,
בהבחנת פרטיות הרבה כידוע
phrases.en: To examine all the different particulars, as is known.

blocks.text: which is the opposite of contraction and squeezing. The *iyun* of *bina*, though at its start it is held in contraction, on one point, at once spreads wide into all its details, examining many particulars: the *Malchus* of *tevuna*, the letters, outer and inner, the angels. That is *hisbonenus*: cutting it up into all its parts. Here it's the opposite: only *daas*, nothing else. If this were a class with students and someone brought up the *Malchus* of *tevuna* now: "Hey, what are you talking? Why are you interrupting the class?"

phrases.he: מה שאין כן הצמצום והכיווץ דהעמקת הדעת,
phrases.en: The *daas* is exactly the opposite;

phrases.he: אדרבה, הוא רק הצמצום,
phrases.en: just the opposite: not to go into all the things, but rather the opposite, to be *metzamtzem* away all the other things,

phrases.he: שהוא הקיבוץ והאסיפה מכל כח שכלו
phrases.en: to focus and gather together the whole power of your brain,

phrases.he: להתקשר רק במושכל זה

blocks.text: The contraction of *ha'amakas hadaas* is, on the contrary, only contraction: squeezing away everything else, gathering the whole power of your brain to connect only with this concept. As we're doing now: "Why are we focusing our whole brain? I mean, there's so many things to think about, and we're thinking only about *daas*." It's exactly the opposite of *bina*.

phrases.he: שזה היפך בחינת התפשטות העיון בהרחבת ענין המושכל,
phrases.en: It's exactly the opposite of analyzing all the different parts.

phrases.he: (בל"א דער קלעפ מיט דעם אריין לייגין זיך גאר כו')
phrases.en: He only busies himself with only this thing, and nothing else.

phrases.he: ואמנם
phrases.en: However,

phrases.he: על ידי העמקת הדעת בא לידי עמקות המושכל עד שרשו בעמקי החכמה ובינה
phrases.en: when you're doing a particular point, you're totally concentrated on that point, and that is what will bring you to the actual *omek* of the *muskal*, all the way to how it is in the *omek* of *chachma* and *bina*.

blocks.text: This is the opposite of the *iyun* spreading out to analyze all the parts. In Yiddish: stuck to it, laying himself into it altogether, busy only with this thing. As we are now with *daas*, putting the whole power of our brain only on it, to the exclusion of everything else.

Yet through *ha'amakas hadaas* one comes to the depth of the concept, *davka* by concentrating on this point. It doesn't mean we'll never learn the other points and stay with this one forever, going over and over it.

Or "we'll sit in a cave in the Himalayas" and go: "*Daas* is delving, *daas* is the concentration of all the powers of your brain, *daas* is the concentration of all the powers of your brain, *daas*..." "That's what they do basically."

sensitivity.reason: Mocks Eastern meditators in a Himalayan cave repeating a phrase.
sensitivity.publishable: It's not that we'll just sit and repeat: "*Daas* is delving, *daas* is the concentration of all the powers of your brain, *daas* is the concentration of all the powers of your brain, *daas*..."

blocks.text: We will get to the other points: the next chapter is about *tevuna*, and then we'll forget about *daas* and concentrate the whole thing *davka* on that. Being totally concentrated on one point is what brings you to the actual depth of the concept, as it is in the depth of *chachma* and *bina*, and in *taalumos chachma*.

phrases.he: (עד בחינת דעת עליון דמזווג חכמה לבינה
phrases.en: This is all the way till the upper *daas*, that is like the *Keser*, which is above *chachma* and *bina* and puts them both together.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב למעלה בענין עומק המושג דבינה,
phrases.en: Like it said before,

phrases.he: והיינו דדעת גנוז בפומא דאימא כו'
phrases.en: *Daas* is hidden inside the mouth of *bina*.

blocks.text: Up to *daas elyon*, which unites *chachma* with *bina*: like the *Keser*, above both, putting them together. With the inner connection you know the thing: you learned it, and now you know it. The *daas tachton* (lower knowledge) is only the *kli*; *daas elyon* means the thing is part of your brain, one thing with you, as "Adam knew Chava": they became one thing. Your whole *chachma* and *bina* are connected together in the *Keser*, as written above about the depth of the concept in *bina*.

And this is *daas* hidden in the mouth of *Ima*, the mouth of *bina*. The mouth is like *Malchus*, the upper *Malchus*: *davka* when you want to say out the *bina*, as we're doing now, you bring the *daas* into it. We weren't concentrating before; now that we want to talk it out, the concentration comes in automatically. "We're not doing like the yogis that we sat down, and now we're going to concentrate." We're trying to understand, and to have a lesson, so the *daas* is revealed, "because that's where it was hidden in the first place."

phrases.he: וכמו שאמרו, משה שהוא הדעת, זכה לבינה שהוא שער הנון,
phrases.en: *Davka* Moshe, which is the *daas*, because he was connected to the *inyan*, that's why he was *zocheh* to the *bina*, which is the *shaar hanun*.

phrases.he: כי הא בהא תליא,
phrases.en: Because *mamash* one depends on the other.

phrases.he: וכמה שכתוב בכתבים בכמה דוכתי ודי למבין.

blocks.text: and as they said, Moshe, who is *daas*: not "a *daas* like the *daas* of the goyim". A Jewish *daas* goes *davka* into the *bina*. "The goyishe *daas*" is a *daas* of *Tohu*, where each *sefira* is on its own, not connected to the others: just concentration. "On what? Well, what do you mean on what? Concentration is just all by itself, right, *Tohu*."

sensitivity.reason: Contrasts a Jewish daas with "the daas of the goyim", a goyishe daas of Tohu.
sensitivity.publishable: **and as they said, Moshe, who is *daas***: this *daas* goes *davka* into the *bina*. A *daas* not connected to *bina* is a *daas* of *Tohu*, where each *sefira* is on its own, not connected to the others: just concentration. "On what? Well, what do you mean on what? Concentration is just all by itself, right, *Tohu*."

blocks.text: So *davka* Moshe, the *daas*, connected to the matter, merited *bina*, the *shaar hanun*: one *mamash* depends on the other. As it says, if there's no *daas* there's no *bina*, and if there's no *bina* there's no *daas* ("I think that's the order, right?"). If you don't concentrate on your lesson, you won't understand nothing; if there's nothing to understand, you lose interest. Without the *daas tachton* of concentrating there's no understanding, and without understanding no *daas elyon*. Concentration with no explanation never goes from *daas tachton* to *daas elyon*: "You'll just sit there and concentrate, and you won't know nothing", and if you do end up knowing something, "it'll just be a vain imagination."

reviewQuestions.question: Why is concentration only a *kli*, "an instrument for an instrument", and what goes wrong when it is taken for the thing itself?
What is a *tamtzis*, and what do instant coffee and knowing how to add show about the depth of the concept?
Why are inventions made by the engineers of a field and not by someone meditating in the Himalayas, and what does the Rebbe Rashab's advice on learning Gemara add?
How is the *navon* higher than the wise man, and what did the Wright brothers see in a bicycle chain?
The text says length and width depend on the depth. What is "the real main point of this chapter" going the other way, and what does it mean for how a student learns?
How is the contraction of deep *daas* the opposite of the spreading of *iyun*, and why does each one need the other?
